passage:
Two weeks ago, Tanvir was, in Sudha's words, "the best human being on the planet". He had lent her his notes when she was ill and walked her to the tuition centre every day. Then, the night before their joint science project was due, with the home printer broken and the shop closing at nine, Tanvir replied "can't come, sorry" when she asked him to bring the charts over. He was at a family dinner.
Sudha stared at the message. "He's a total traitor," she typed to her cousin. "He only ever cared about himself. I was stupid to trust him." She printed the charts herself at the shop two minutes before closing, fuming.
The next morning Tanvir arrived early with a box of laddoos from the dinner and the charts laminated. Sudha didn't know where to put her anger.

qa.q: What did Tanvir reply when Sudha asked him to bring the charts?
qa.a: "can't come, sorry"

qa.q: Why did Sudha go from 'best human being' to 'total traitor' so fast?
qa.a: Deadline stress made one small letdown feel huge, and her strong feelings left no room to hold Tanvir's kindness and this one miss together.

qa.q: What could Sudha say to Tanvir the next morning?
qa.a: Something honest but fair, like 'I was really stressed last night and got angry; thanks for the charts', which holds both sides of him.

qa.q: How might Tanvir feel if he knew what Sudha had typed about him?
qa.a: Hurt and confused, since he only missed one evening for a family dinner and still came early with the charts laminated.

grounding: Under deadline pressure a teenager flips from calling a friend perfect to calling him a traitor after one small letdown.

subtype: Friend all good then all bad [Actor]
passage:
Preeti used to say Vijay was "literally perfect". They had been best friends since Class 7 in their Pune housing society: same bus, same terrible jokes, same seat in the library. Then on Tuesday, at the society's Ganpati dance practice, Vijay laughed when someone mocked her step. Just one laugh.
By Tuesday night Preeti had deleted their photos from her phone. "He's fake," she told her mother. "He was always fake. He only pretended to like me."
Her mother asked, "Always? What about when he sat with you at the hospital after your fall?"
Preeti opened her mouth, shut it, and stomped off to her room. She lay on the bed, remembering the hospital and the laugh at the same time, and couldn't make them fit.

qa.q: What did Preeti delete on Tuesday night?
qa.a: Their photos from her phone.

qa.q: Why does it feel so convincing to Preeti that Vijay 'was always fake'?
qa.a: The laugh hurt so much that it seemed to rewrite everything; strong feelings made it hard to hold the good memories and the disappointment together.

qa.q: What choice by her mother helped Preeti start to see both sides?
qa.a: Asking about one specific good memory, the hospital visit, instead of arguing, which left Preeti holding both pictures of Vijay. 🙂

qa.q: How might Vijay feel the next day when Preeti turns cold?
qa.a: Confused and hurt, perhaps not even realising his one laugh stung so much, and unsure how to fix it.

grounding: A teenager decides her once-perfect best friend was always fake after one hurtful laugh, and struggles to fit the good and bad memories together.

subtype: Friend all good then all bad [Actor]
passage:
On the school bus, Monday.
"Kashish! You saved me a seat! You're the best. You're honestly my favourite person in this whole school."
"It's just a seat, Avni."
The next Monday, same bus.
"Avni, I saved you a seat."
"Don't bother."
"What? What happened?"
"You told Rhea about my Hindi marks. You're a snake. You've always been a snake."
"I said you were worried about Hindi. I was asking Rhea to help you."
"Oh, so now you're a saint?"
"No. I'm not a saint and I'm not a snake. I'm just your friend who made a mistake."
Avni looked out of the window. The bus lurched over a speed-breaker.
"...You did help me with fractions last week."
"I did."
"I'm still annoyed."
"That's fair. You can be annoyed and still sit here."
Avni sat.

qa.q: What did Avni accuse Kashish of telling Rhea about?
qa.a: Avni's Hindi marks.

qa.q: Why did Avni jump from 'favourite person' to 'snake' so quickly?
qa.a: Feeling exposed about the Hindi marks hurt so much that Kashish suddenly seemed all bad, and the earlier kindness vanished from view.

qa.q: What turning point on the bus helped Avni hold both sides of Kashish?
qa.a: Kashish refusing both labels, 'not a saint and not a snake', which let Avni remember the fractions help while still being annoyed.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel being called a snake after saving a seat?
qa.a: Hurt and unfairly judged, since Kashish meant to help; staying calm and honest probably took real effort.

grounding: A teenager swings from calling a friend the best to calling them a snake after a small slight, until the friend refuses both labels.

subtype: Friend all good then all bad [Actor]
passage:
Last March, if you'd asked me, I'd have said Neelam was the most perfect friend in the world. She shared her headphones on every bus ride, did my hair for annual day, and knew what I was thinking before I did. I wrote her name inside my compass box.
Then on my fifteenth birthday she didn't message me until nine at night. Nine. I checked my phone all day. By evening, in my head, she had become a fake, a traitor, someone who had probably never liked me. I told two girls she was "two-faced" and scratched her name out of the compass box.
Her message, when it came, said: "Sorry Gargi, Nani was in hospital all day."
I'm sixteen now. I still feel that switch sometimes, all good to all bad in one second. I'm learning to wait before I scratch anything out.

qa.q: When did Neelam message Gargi on the birthday?
qa.a: Not until nine at night.

qa.q: Why did Neelam go from perfect to "a traitor" so fast in Gargi's mind?
qa.a: The hurt of waiting all day was so strong that Gargi couldn't hold Neelam's good sides and this one disappointment together, so the whole picture flipped.

qa.q: What is Gargi learning to do when the switch comes?
qa.a: To wait before scratching anything out, giving time to find out what really happened before deciding a friend is all bad.

qa.q: What might Neelam feel on hearing she'd been called "two-faced"?
qa.a: Neelam, who had spent the day at the hospital with Nani, would likely feel hurt and confused at being judged so harshly for a late message.

grounding: Shows a teenager who sees a friend as perfect and then as a traitor after one late birthday message, unable in that moment to hold both sides together.

subtype: Friend all good then all bad [Actor]
passage:
School counsellor's note, Noor, Class 9
Thomas came in on Tuesday, sent by his class teacher after an argument in the corridor. Two weeks ago, in this same room, he described Akshay as "basically the perfect friend, never lets anyone down". Today Akshay was "a snake", "fake from the start", "the worst person in the school". The reason: Akshay had picked someone else as his partner for the science fair.
Thomas talked fast, fists tight. I didn't argue. I asked him to tell me three things Akshay had done this year. He listed them: stood up for him when seniors took his bat, shared notes when he had jaundice, and chose a different partner. He went quiet. "Two good, one bad," he said. "I guess he's not a snake."
Next: meet Thursday; suggest Thomas tell Akshay directly that he felt left out.

qa.q: Why was Akshay "the worst person in the school" to Thomas that day?
qa.a: Akshay had picked someone else as his partner for the science fair.

qa.q: Why did one slight wipe out everything good for Thomas?
qa.a: Feeling left out hurt so much that he couldn't hold Akshay's kindness and this disappointment at the same time, so Akshay flipped from perfect to a snake.

qa.q: What did Noor's "three things" question do well?
qa.a: It helped Thomas lay the good and the disappointing side by side himself, so he could see Akshay as a whole person again.

qa.q: How might Akshay feel if Thomas says he felt left out, instead of calling him a snake?
qa.a: Akshay would probably understand and feel less attacked, and could explain the choice or include Thomas next time.

grounding: Illustrates, in a counsellor's note, a teenager who swings from calling a friend perfect to calling him a traitor over one small slight, and begins to hold both sides.
